extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, journalists, and media practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles about how public opinion is formed, sustained, and enlisted through media, stereotypes, storytelling, and psychological biases, as discussed in Lippmann's Public Opinion. Useful for evaluating or producing news, political propaganda, and popular representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption is against our having picked true samples if we are acting on a casual impression; we are so little trained in the selection of our samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from a few concordant acquaintances or isolated instances — e.g., when the first six people we meet agree with us they may all have read the same newspaper. Estimating probabilities requires proper sampling (cannot send out a questionnaire to 816 random samples every time, but casual impressions are unreliable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid post hoc/illusory causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking causes and effects of unseen and complicated affairs, haphazard opinion is very tricky; the commonest form of reasoning is the intuitive, post hoc ergo propter hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer causation simply because two events occur together or in sequence — especially when events are attended through stereotypes or limited access to information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional association bias (affect-driven linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two ideas that come together arouse the same feeling, they are likely to be accepted as causally connected; powerful feeling attached to one idea will summon any idea that feels the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary that 'everything painful tends to collect into one system of cause and effect, and likewise everything pleasant.' Examples: smallpox ↔ alehouses; Relativity ↔ Bolshevism. Emotion can embed ludicrous entanglements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward absolutism in public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion prefers absolute statements and dislikes qualifying adverbs; people prefer 'most' to 'more' and avoid words like rather, perhaps, if, or, but, toward, not quite, almost, temporarily, partly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly every opinion about public affairs needs qualifying words to be accurate, but public taste favors absolutes (one hundred percent, everywhere, forever). Writers should consciously deflate absolutist claims with qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and dramatization (allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: To enlist interest, abstractions (Social Movements, Economic Forces, National Interests, Public Opinion) are treated as persons and dramatized; names become personified (e.g., John Bull).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate abstract public affairs into humanized, dramatized images so audiences can identify and participate; this aids attention and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete visual metaphors and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Human qualities ascribed to impressions tend to be visualized in physical metaphors (migration as river or flood; courage as rock; purpose as road).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot be omnipresent or omniscient, visualization and pictorial representations (pictures, headlines, films, cartoons) are the surest way to convey ideas and make them emotionally accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of identifiable heroes/villains in popular representation
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked; you know who the hero is at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass-audience works succeed when identification is clear; lack of definite marking reduces popular appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience something to do (exercise the love of struggle or passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do; the audience must be exercised by the image through themes that arouse strong responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two dominant forms of exercise are sexual passion and fighting; political interest is sustained by an issue or fight. If no pugnacity is enlisted, distant problems fail to hold general attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create suspense via struggle, antagonist, and obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense constitutes the difference between low and high popular appeal; motion pictures and popular stories draw and hold attention because they depict unfolding events with struggle and an outcome to await.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To increase engagement: add an antagonist, add an obstacle, add a problem, emphasize the spectator's questions — these techniques transform passive viewing into active suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance realism and romanticism in narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular taste prefers drama that originates in a realistic setting (for plausible identification) and ends in a romantic setting (desirable but not inconceivable); pure fantasy or relentless realism fail to satisfy large audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin plausibly, allow liberal canons between, and deliver a satisfying (romantic) resolution. Producers often must adhere to familiar stereotypes to ensure financial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic constraints and reliance on stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because investments (films, periodicals) demand instant and widespread popularity, producers must adhere to the stereotypes they find or risk failure; stereotypes can be altered but not quickly enough to guarantee commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that managers and editors protect investments by avoiding risky departures; pioneering artists who alter stereotypes face economic penalties even if artistically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagandist formula: plausible beginning then optimistic future
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilful propagandist starts with a plausible analysis (foothold in reality) and then abandons prolonged analysis, stoking energy by brandishing a 'passport to heaven' or an optimistic future (happy ending) to sustain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula works when the public fiction meshes with private urgency; it deliberately minimizes tedium of real political accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience heterogeneity reduces shared meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: As the audience grows larger and more mixed, the number of common words and shared concrete factors diminishes; common factors become more abstract and the story is interpreted differently by diverse individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater variation in response with larger, more mixed audiences; messaging that appeals broadly must rely on more abstract or widely shared handles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories and rumors are reworked by retelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The original story grows and changes as each narrator edits and revises it; printed records check exuberance, but rumor grows wings and acquires additions as it is retold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News and public narratives undergo continual alteration; producers and analysts must account for transmission effects (distortion through gossip and retelling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and tactile value are prerequisites for shared understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: No idea is lucid for practical decision until it has visual or tactile value; intuition alone is often private and incommunicable, so ideas must be made visual or tactile to enable collective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When action depends on many people sharing an idea, give the idea concrete visual handles that allow identification and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which 'self' is engaged determines self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-interest determines opinion only when we know which self (one of many possible selves) is engaged; different selves (patriot, employer, lover, proprietor) mobilize different impulses and thus different opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand or influence public opinion, identify which self a message invokes (e.g., economic self vs. outraged family-head) because that changes the intensity and content of response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation-dependent variability of character and disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's character and the selves that appear vary with time, circumstance, and social expectations; unexpected situations reveal dispositions otherwise latent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions are not fixed traits of persons but situational expressions; analysts should avoid treating 'self-interest' as a single static variable.
